title: Notes of Ministry - 43 - June 1976

paragraphs.text: Genesis 24: 62–I carry a remark made in the reading as to the degree to which our actual experience of the headship of Christ would lead us to apprehend what He Himself is engaged with. One longs to know it; one longs for the brethren to know it. It is an interesting and observable fact that most of the time when we speak about headship we speak as if its intention was to adjust us. I think it is a question whether the headship of Christ ever adjusts us, or rather whether it does not require an adjusted state for the headship of Christ to operate. It was said in the reading that His headship and His lordship run very close together, and they do, and we perhaps do not always distinguish the way in which He serves us in one connection from the way in which He serves us in the other.

Isaac here is active. It is “toward the beginning of evening”—it represents the present time; it always has represented the present time. There has never been a time since the Spirit came when it has not been towards the beginning of evening. The expectation that the Spirit’s day would end and Christ have what is His has always been the impression which lay upon the saints. But here Isaac comes from the well Beer-lahai-roi, the ‘well of the Living who was seen (or ‘Who reveals himself’)’ (see note to Genesis 16: 14). What an area Christ moves in! He moves in relation to the Spirit, not the Spirit as against the flesh (see Galatians 5: 17) or that order of things, but the Spirit as bearing on us in relation to the revelation of God. What a sphere Christ’s thoughts are occupied with! It is from that that He proceeds to meditate in the fields at the beginning of evening.

One longs to know what Christ meditates on at the present time. Do you think He meditates on the failure of the saints, or the breakdown of the church in its public position? I do not think so. I think He meditates on what He is about to receive—in this chapter Isaac is about to receive Rebecca. We do not know how long the servant had been away, how long the journey took. It is left like that so that we should not know, so that we should not be able to calculate how long the day of the Spirit’s service is; but Isaac here is expectant and he went out to meditate. How much in a certain sense one would give to know what was in Isaac’s mind at this time. He went out to meditate in the fields. Think of that—Isaac meditating in the fields—the vast area over which Christ is able to look as He meditates at the present time. What an area it is! The earth is His; He looks over it. God has said to Him as His Son that He would give Him the “nations for an inheritance, and for thy possession the ends of the earth”, Psalm 2: 8. He goes out into the fields to meditate, fields which He is about to have in their totality as His own, fields which have been the area of the operations of God, out of which in our own day the Spirit is operating to secure the assembly, on which in another day God has operated with an earthly family and with other families to secure them all for Christ in the day when He has what is His, “For the earth is the Lord’s”, 1 Corinthians 10: 26. He went out into that area, that
wide area, to meditate.

We were speaking on Wednesday evening here about the city in the world to come and how it seems that God’s thoughts in relation to every dispensation are gathered up there, without distinguishing one dispensation from another very much; but in the world to come as it is presented in Revelation 21 you get some impression of I AM, the One who has been the same through all dispensations and who gathers up everything in a vessel that can be for the glory of God. What wide operations God has had in what the fields speak of! Think of the reference to “a field which Jehovah has blessed” (Genesis 27: 27); that I think, beloved, is the area that Christ is peculiarly occupied with at the present time. Ruth was bidden to concentrate on “the field which is being reaped” (Ruth 2: 9), but Christ has all the fields before Him, and out of them He is going to have what is for Himself. I believe He meditates on that at the present time; not on failure, not on Adam’s sin, not on the breakdown of Cain in relation to Abel, not on Abraham’s failures in going down to Egypt, not on Isaac’s failures in going down to Egypt, not on Israel’s failures in turning away from God and from the law, but on “whose is the adoption … and the promises … and of whom, as according to flesh, is the Christ”, Romans 9: 4, 5. This, I think, is the anti-type of the area of Isaac’s meditation in the fields towards the beginning of evening. And especially upon the assembly; not the assembly as it is publicly, as one of the hymns we used to have at school says—‘By schisms rent asunder, by heresies distressed’—not like that. No, He has gone out to meditate on what is intrinsically fair; as far as could be said of what is creature, intrinsically perfect, for you only have to look back earlier in this chapter to discover the characteristics of Rebecca,

and as far as it may be said of what is creature she was perfect. No one had ever known her; she was perfect, representing the assembly just kept for Christ. That is, I believe, what He meditates on at the present time; and, beloved, He would draw us by His headship into what is occupying Him. One says elsewhere—“My meditation of him shall be sweet” (Psalm 104: 34. A.V.), but think of meditating with Him! Think of meditating with Christ over what He is so soon going to have, as the beginning of evening gives way to the evening; and the evening does not give way to the night, the evening gives way to the day, and then He will have what the Spirit has been diligent to secure.

Christ comes, as I say, from this particular area of the Spirit in relation to the revelation of God. How it bears on the present day! What fulness there is in it, what Isaac may meditate on in regard to the God who reveals Himself, the Living One who is seen. How much Christ has to reflect on in that, how much He has in relation to the Spirit, in relation to His own part, and in relation to the Father. But then, “In the fields toward the beginning of evening”. What is about to happen? He is about to have the assembly in its blessedness, in its fairness and perfection, in its suitability for Him, in a state where without any further preparation she can just be taken into His own sphere. He meditates on that. Beloved, may we learn to meditate on it; may we learn to have our thoughts lifted above the level of things on which we live so much. Our minds still revert to administration as if it was the main occupation of the saints, but Christ is meditating on what He will administer, on a sphere of things that will be in His hand because the Father loves Him, and has given everything to be in His hand because He loves Him. He meditates on all
that He will have.

Well, beloved, may our own thoughts be drawn into His. David did not send for Abigail to tell her about Nabal. He sent for Abigail to commune with her that she might become his wife (see 1 Samuel 25: 39); and Christ as typified in Isaac meditates on what He will soon have out of all the fields, what He will have out of this field which is blessedly being reaped at the present time, the assembly apart from breakdown or failure or sorrow. May our thoughts be lifted up to the level on which He Himself is occupied. May we learn His headship in that sphere, where He would draw us into, one might almost say, the relish with which He reflects on what has been secured through God’s operations in all the fields, but what He will have blessedly out of this field of the present moment in the assembly.

These scriptures bring before us persons who returned. We have seen many depart, even disciples, as in John 6. They are said to be disciples of Jesus, who went away. The Lord was affected by their going away and showed His concern for the apostles. At that point He said, “Will ye also go away?”. It is a time of returning. The Lord healed ten lepers, but only one returned, of whom

He said, “There have not been found to return and give glory to God save this stranger”, Luke 17: 18. Persons who return value their own blessing, but there is something more than our own blessing. We would surely desire to be among those who return to give glory to God.

In His ways with us God brings about conditions which may awaken our consciences. It is all of His grace if He does that. He may cause report to reach our ears. Evidently it was so with Naomi. It says that, “she had heard in the fields of Moab how that Jehovah had visited his people to give them bread”. Dear brethren, we are in such a time as that. God is visiting His people to give them bread. None of us can live without bread. The Lord Jesus is the bread of God (John 6: 33). There is no better food upon which to feed and I believe that God would make His people aware everywhere, not only that He has visited them, but that it is in order to give them bread. Well, this brought about a change in these women, desolate though they were. It says of Naomi that “she arose, she and her daughters-in-law, and returned from the fields of Moab”. It is a great thing to reach that point in our exercises. The younger son in Luke 15 made a spiritual resolution, “I will rise up and go to my father”, Luke 15: 18. No transport was provided for him; it was his own exercise to return. I wonder if such an exercise is to be found in all our hearts. Another prophet says, “If ye will inquire, inquire; return, come”, Isaiah 21: 12.

Well, they began to return. Three of them began, and two of them finished. Things test you immediately you are set to return. You will find that nature’s claims will test you. Orpah fell a prey to nature’s claims. She went back to her

people and to her gods. What is natural is sometimes very close to what is idolatrous and, alas, Orpah went back to both. But Naomi and Ruth returned. Naomi says, “Jehovah has brought me home again empty” (Ruth 1: 21). That is a beautiful expression, “brought me home again”. Of course we have to understand that spiritually, what home is. The disciples of John who followed Jesus asked, “Rabbi … where abidest thou? He says to them, Come and see. They went therefore, and saw where he abode; and they abode with him that day. It was about the tenth hour”, John 1: 38, 39. It is a wonderful thing to find the Lord has a home, not only in heaven, but here upon earth. Every true believer has to find that he cannot be satisfied until he finds where Jesus dwells in what we may speak of as His home conditions.

The second passage we read again speaks of returning persons. “The children of Israel shall come, they and the children of Judah together”. It is a wonderful thing to come into the stream of returning persons. Does any one of us think we have never strayed? “For ye were going astray as sheep, but have now returned to the shepherd and overseer of your souls”, 1 Peter 2: 25. It is time we all returned. Now the prophet says that this return takes place “In those days”. The preceding verses show that those were the days in which God was breaking down the power of Babylon, as in the present day also He is breaking down the power of Babylon. Where is He doing that? He is doing it in the souls of His people. If His people are in Babylon His word for them is, “Come out of her, my people, that ye have not fellowship in her sins”, Revelation 18: 4. Returning persons are well aware that the judgment of God is about to fall upon this modern Babylon.

“Her sins”, the scripture says, “have been heaped on one another up to the heaven”, Revelation 18: 5. Understand, these are not your sins or my sins. The Lord says to one woman, “Thy sins are forgiven”, Luke 7: 48. Maybe every person here knows that his or her sins are forgiven; but here the Spirit of God speaks of Babylon’s sins which “have been heaped on one another up to the heaven”. So He says, “Come out of her”, out of that idolatrous system where the ruling word is luxury. How it describes the materialism of the present time! Light from God will cause you to arrive at a judgment of it so that as to Babylon the word is, “God has judged your judgment upon her”, Revelation 18: 20. God will deal with Babylon, but we are to come out of her. Many attractive things, music and art, luxury, all these things, go to make up Babylon. She lives luxuriously. God says, “Come out of her, my people”.

You may say, ‘Where am I to come?’. Well now, look at these people. “They shall inquire concerning Zion, with their faces thitherward”. Zion is David’s city, where he had a stronghold, and where he lived. We come again to the thought of a home, and that Christ has conditions in which He dwells. He dwells in the hearts of those who love Him, who love Him “more than these”, John 21: 15. At the end of John’s gospel the Lord’s question to Peter was, “Lovest thou me more than these?”. Now that word “these” can mean things as well as persons. Peter thought he loved the Lord more than the other disciples and he had to find that the spirit was willing but the flesh was weak. We, too, have to find that the flesh is weak. Not only is it wilful, but it is weak. The Lord says, ‘Do you love Me more than these?’—these things—this hobby, or that pastime that you would like to follow. These are challenging matters, are they
not? We should love Christ more than anyone, and more than anything else. We should love Him most.

Now, these returning persons are like that; they are inquiring concerning Zion. A christian said to me recently, ‘Do you think there is a collective position now?’. ‘Oh, yes’, I replied, ‘I am sure there is’. It is a wonderful thing that it is so. It is not the Lord’s thought that we should be stranded as individualists. These returning persons are returning together, inquiring concerning Zion with their faces thitherward. Which way are you looking? Lot’s wife looked back. Persons who look back finally go back. The thing is to inquire concerning Zion and have your face thitherward.

Jesus drew near to two in Luke 24 who were going away. He made their heart burn within them and they returned to Jerusalem the same hour—no hesitation, no delay. What did they find? The eleven gathered together; a company with the greatest light on earth at that time saying, “The Lord is indeed risen and has appeared to Simon”, Luke 24: 34. Think of coming into a company as returning persons and finding that! Now this involves determination and committal. These returning persons are saying something, “Come, and let us join ourselves to Jehovah”. That is the whole point. Your link with Christ is to be renewed from your side. “He that is joined to the Lord is one Spirit”, 1 Corinthians 6: 17. Some are concerned as to which company they should join. “Let us join ourselves to Jehovah, in an everlasting covenant that shall not be forgotten”. That is committal, and a necessary thing on the part of every returning person.
Now just a word about this woman in Kings.

God in His ways had caused a famine to come, and such experiences come into the lives of most of us. There is an element in this woman of obedience, although the ways of God with her might seem to be adverse. She was to go and dwell in the land of the Philistines for seven years. At the end of seven years the woman returned and cried to the king for her house and for her land. Every believer has a right to share the portion of the saints in light. The inheritance belongs to them. This woman was concerned about her inheritance. The king and Gehazi were just occupied in anecdotes, certain things that are reported. We hear—and thank God for them!—reports of persons being recovered, of sons being restored to life. Gehazi and the king were speaking in an academic way about these things when suddenly the woman and her son appeared. There was the evidence substantially in living persons, one restored to life, the other returning to take up her inheritance.

Then the word in regard of the woman was, “Restore all that was hers”. What grace! What time has been wasted, dear brethren, in what is trivial. Let us waste no more time. The greatest things are within our reach on the principle of desire, and Christ died and the Holy Spirit has been given that we might come into possession of them. It says that the woman cried unto the king for her house and for her land. We need to be strengthened in depth of desire and exercise to come into possession of what we are entitled to. Title is one thing; to take possession of what is yours in title is another. “Restore all that was hers, and all the revenue of the land since the day that she left the country even until now”—the capital and the interest. She is thus no longer at a disadvantage: with her house and with her land she can serve God. Lydia said, “If ye have
judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house” (Acts 16: 15), and then, as in Martha’s house, there would be the service of God.

These are great things, dear brethren, which are open to returning persons, and what I plead for is more exercise, more concern, that we should retrace our steps, not to take up any mere religious position, for God says through His prophet, “If thou wilt return ... return unto me”, Jeremiah 4: 1. It is to that living link and the enjoyment of it that the return is to be, that we should join ourselves to Him in an everlasting covenant, for “he that is joined to the Lord is one Spirit”. May it be so for His name’s sake.

articles.title: “A TIME TO SEEK, AND A TIME TO LOSE”
articles.author: W. S. Chellberg

paragraphs.text: It is a time to lose. It is interesting the way that the wise preacher says it, “A time to seek, and a time to lose”. Then he says, “A time to keep”. I think I would have said, ‘It is a time to keep, and a time to lose’, ‘but he says it is a time to seek, and a time to lose, and I think that is the gospel. That is the present day; it is a time to seek. And the Lord says, “whosoever shall lose his life for my sake”. We do not often think of that in connection with the gospel, losing, but it is an interesting thought. The preacher brings it in, and the wisdom of Solomon is amazing as we

read this book. He says interesting things. He says in another place, “I turned, I and my heart”, Ecclesiastes 7: 25. So I trust that that may be so this afternoon in relation to the gospel, that I might turn, “I and my heart”. That is, that something will happen in my heart in relation to God and in relation to Jesus.

So Jesus says, “Whosoever shall lose his life for my sake, he shall save it”. Men are greatly concerned about saving their lives, and in a human sense that is right; in regard of others that would be my action, I would desire to aid in any way to save a life; and that would first be in relation to eternal things. It is an awful thing to think of a person who dies, in some cases in a violent way, thrust, you might say, into eternity; young people thrust into eternity, persons in the prime of their life thrust into eternity, suddenly. Scripture speaks about that, “then sudden destruction comes”, 1 Thessalonians 5: 3. You cannot but be affected as you think of it in regard of men, in regard of the world around, even perhaps persons you know—thrust into eternity. The scripture says the pitcher is shattered at the fountain (Ecclesiastes 12: 6). That is a chapter for young people, beginning, “Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth”, but it also says, “before … the pitcher be shattered at the fountain”. The fountain is the spring of things, it could refer to the prime of life; but “the pitcher is shattered”.

So we begin by thinking of persons seeking to save their lives, and they do all manner of things to attain their goals. Men set high goals; young people in this present day are setting goals, even the young people here set goals for themselves. That is, you have some thought of what you want to do, what you want to be when you finish school,

when you get to a certain age. Set your goals in relation to the things of God, in relation to the sufferings of the man Christ Jesus. I would just urge you to do that. Do not have divergent goals, aims, or objectives, but set your goal, set your heart, in relation to God’s things. You may say, ‘Well, you are not so very old so you do not know’, but I believe that those who are older here today would agree with that. Set your mind and your aim in the way of God’s things; that is the way to save your life in the sense of what the Lord is saying here, “he shall save it”. The Lord says, “Seek ye first the kingdom of God … and all these things shall be added unto you”, Matthew 6: 33. It is a hard thing for younger persons; I know because it has been a hard thing for me to learn, that one is to be content with clothing and shelter and food. Be content; we are so prone to be energized by this present materialistic world where things have to be better and better, and the best, and the most, and the biggest; but that is not the gospel—that is not God’s way. So as we follow what the Lord says here, the thought is the saving of life, but how do you arrive at that?

The world has its own ideas of how to become a millionaire in three years on real estate. I read that book, and other books like it—‘How to be a Success in Business’. That is the world’s way of saving your life, but the end is “the penalty of the loss of himself”. So I would just urge everyone to pause at the present moment in relation to the gospel, “the glad tidings of the glory of the blessed God”, 1 Timothy 1: 11. Think of how God has come out to us, how He has given everything; think of God giving His Son, Jesus. Think of the sacrifice that it was to God to give His own Son, as the parable that the Lord spoke indicates. The vineyard owner said, Well, I will send my son

and they will have respect for him. But they took him, they cast him out, and they killed him (Matthew 21: 37–39). How awful it is! Well, let us allow the sufferings of Jesus to bear into our hearts. I would suggest that we all read where Jesus was before Pilate; read it slowly and consider what it meant to Him to be before that governor, to have false witnesses brought against Him, to be spit upon, and to be hit, struck in the face; “his visage was so marred more than any man”, it says (Isaiah 52: 14). Think of the sufferings of Jesus. Oh if they could just bear into our hearts, how Jesus went to that cross, the suffering of it, the way that He went, and what He did. He went that way in His love. He went that way that you and I might be secured.

Now I trust as we consider this it will strike a note in our hearts regarding Jesus. I trust that it may strike through into your heart this afternoon, as you think about it. Think of Jesus hanging on that cross, and they said, “He saved others; let him save himself”, Luke 23: 35. Oh the hardness of men! He would not save Himself, He would not save Himself. Why? It was because of you. It was because of me. He said, “It is finished”. Oh think of those hours on the cross; think of the suffering that He endured for your sake. When you think of that how can you want to save your life? Are you prepared to seek and to lose? “Seek ye first the kingdom of God” (Matthew 6: 33); that is what Jesus says. I trust everyone here is, and will be as the days go on, more prepared to seek and to lose, to lose all that men want you to be. You might lose that title, you might lose that thing that is looming so big in the world, that they want you to be, or that they think you could do. You lose that in view of Him. You lose that in view of another
life.

Well, I trust that we may, each one, be stimulated in this line. Usually we do not speak about losing things; we speak about gaining things, and in christianity you gain a Saviour, you gain eternal life—“that they may lay hold of what is really life”, 1 Timothy 6: 19. The world has its own idea about life, they have what they call life, the jet set or whatever they call it; the bright lights and the music, and the hustle and bustle; they call it life—it is certainly not eternal life. I trust we each one may be stimulated and encouraged to lay hold of what is really life; lose whatever else is there, lose what stands in the way. “What shall a man profit?” Well, you sit down and figure it out; the corporate head may earn four or five hundred thousand dollars—you think, ‘That is for me’. Then you figure it out, and you say, ‘How does this stand up? So I have this job and I have it for five, eight, ten years, and I suffer the loss of my own soul; is it worth it?’ Will you suffer the loss of your soul to go in for something else? I trust there is no one here who would do that. Lose those things, and seek what is of God.

Let us, dear brethren, allow our hearts to be affected by the sufferings of that Man, Jesus, as He went to the cross. Why did He do it? All these questions you have to answer yourself, you see; you determine to lose certain things and to seek other things, and “he shall save it”. I trust that everyone here will be saved. I trust you have a Saviour. Now that is something that is right to ask, and I ask it often, and I trust you will answer it. Are you saved? Do you have a Saviour? It is a constant desire of God—Are you saved? The apostle says, “Knowing therefore the terror of

the Lord we persuade men”, 2 Corinthians 5: 11. Think of the greatness and the almightiness of God, the surety and the verity of His word, that what He has said will come to pass, “and forasmuch as it is the portion of men once to die”, once to die, “and after this the judgment”, Hebrews 9: 27.

Well, these things all come into the gospel, and we need the warning, but I trust that we will be encouraged as we think of the sufferings of Christ. It says elsewhere that God will “judge the habitable earth ... by the man whom he has appointed”, Acts 17: 31. Thank God for that Man! I trust that everyone here knows that Man, and loves that Man—Jesus, and will aspire (in a right way) to save his life and not suffer the loss of his own soul. Just these few words, but I trust that they have gone into your heart and will produce a result for God. It is “a time to seek, and a time to lose”, and I trust we will be active in it, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: THE FRUITS OF GRIEF
articles.author: D. Wright
articles.meeting: Substance of word in meeting for ministry

paragraphs.text: Each of these passages speaks of the matter of grief. Not that I want to engage the beloved brethren with grief, far otherwise. But there are to be positive results Godward from the grief which God in His infinite wisdom allows. There is much in the way of grief weighing heavily on the spirits of the saints at the present time, and I believe that God intends to use it to increase our knowledge of Himself, hence the importance of being with Him in whatever experiences He may pass us through.

In the first epistle to the Corinthians Paul had faithfully to draw attention to sins of a most serious nature that were prevalent amongst them. So the apostle says in the verses we read that he did not regret it if that letter had grieved them. Then he says, “Now I rejoice, not that ye have been grieved, but that ye have been grieved to repentance”. Think of the joy it gave the apostle that to a large degree repentance had come in as a result of his faithful speaking. How much failure had come in in Corinth. How much failure has come in in our own assembly history. How much failure has come in in our individual histories. Repentance would mean that the Corinthians would have the same judgment as God in regard to what had been among them. Repentance is very real, and involves a deep relationship with God Himself. The working out of it would involve grief; but “grief according to God works repentance to salvation, never to be regretted”. So the positive result is that you can look back on an experience with God and you can say that, although painful at the time, it was an experience that you will never regret having. So the passage goes on to say, “But the grief of the world works death”. Grief gone through without God brings in bitterness. But as gone through with Him it draws us closer to the One who loves us, and brings us into a new-found joy as repentance is arrived at.
In Hebrews 12 it is a matter of grief not caused by our failure, but because of the Father’s chastening. He may use discipline in our circumstances

to chasten us that there may be more fruit to Him. The Lord says, “As to every branch in me not bearing fruit, he takes it away; and as to every one bearing fruit, he purges it that it may bring forth more fruit”, John 15: 2. If anything of self has to go it brings in grief. So it says, “But no chastening at the time seems to be matter of joy, but of grief; but afterwards yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness”. Thus you get a positive result again. Then it adds, “to those exercised by it”. That implies that we are not to be casual but are to relate ourselves to God. So our own personal link with the Father, and with the Lord Jesus, is strengthened, knowing that what lies behind the Father’s chastening is His love.

Finally, in 1 Peter we have “for a little while at present, if needed, put to grief by various trials”, or as the footnote says, ‘temptations’. These are things we are constantly surrounded by in the wilderness. Peter writes to the sojourners of the dispersion. The saints were scattered, as in the present day. Peter first of all reminds them of what lay before them. He speaks of “a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from among the dead … an incorruptible and undefiled and unfailing inheritance, reserved in the heavens for you”. We need, beloved brethren, to remind each other more of the hope that lies before us, that of seeing Jesus face to face. We may tend to be occupied much with history and what is past, but what is far greater lies before us. John in Revelation 21 speaks of the way that God Himself “shall wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death shall not exist any more, nor grief, nor cry, nor distress shall exist any more, for the former things have passed away”. What a day that will be when grief shall not exist any more! What a joy to know that there

is an inheritance reserved in the heavens for you. You may go into a hall and see the word ‘Reserved’ on a particular seat; it is reserved for a particular person. Well, your inheritance is reserved for you, and in this sense it is exclusively for you. In John 14: 2 the Lord says, “In my Father’s house there are many abodes; were it not so, I had told you—for I go to prepare you a place”.

There is much grief at the present time, showing that the present day is one of education, and growth. We will not have to do with God in regard of these things in a coming day, but we do now, and God intends that there should be formation according to Himself by means of what He allows us to pass through in His infinite wisdom. May we thus value the present time, and may the Lord encourage all our hearts, for His name’s sake.

The Supper is a heart matter. The Lord speaks thus to the heart of the assembly. The language of Hosea 2: 14–23 can be taken up in the light of the assembly and her relations with Christ. The enjoyment of our inheritance, our ‘vineyards’, flows out from the Supper, the place where the Lord gathers us in the wilderness. Responsive singing, as with Israel in Exodus 15, and the understanding of relationship expressed in the words “My husband”, indicate betrothal. “I will sow her unto me in the land” suggests the fruitfulness that is for God, not

now just “her vineyards”, but God’s inheritance secured in the land of His purpose. All is on the basis of mercy, “God being rich in mercy”, Ephesians 2: 4. There is peculiar freshness about recovery days, resulting in God owning “Thou art my people”—He is not ashamed of them—and in our owning Him in language corresponding with what was found uniquely on the lips of Jesus—“My God”.

FRAGRANCE FOR GOD Paul says, “We are a sweet odour of Christ to God”, 2 Corinthians 2: 15. Wherever you think of the apostle—serving among the saints; in his prayers and communion; in peril and shipwreck; in the loneliness of prison life; combating evil and error—the odour of Christ was there. God had in him the continuance in character of the fragrance which ascended to Him from the life of Christ in all the varied circumstances of His service here. The holy anointing oil (Exodus 30: 22–33) with its five ingredients, each present in divinely ordered proportion, is a type of the perfect blending in Christ of all that is delightful to God in manhood. Olive oil was one of the elements, speaking of the Holy Spirit’s service that there may be the continuance in the saints, for divine pleasure, of the fragrance of that dependent Man.

There is no odour for divine pleasure in what marks us naturally—disobedience, discontent, earthliness, selfishness—but the Spirit would ever engage us with Christ and thus produce in us features that carry the holy, fragrant odour of that Man. It is as if the Father would say, ‘I
have had this in Jesus, and now I have it also in My people’.

So many things have been forgotten! The readings and addresses that the Lord is giving us at this moment provide an opportunity for the Spirit to bring out things that have been there all the time; none of the words of Jesus can be lost, hence the importance of such meetings. Brethren coming together in dependence on the Lord give the Comforter such an opportunity. He is here in the name of Christ, teaching us all things, and bringing to our remembrance all the things that the Lord has said to us.

Leaven should never be found in our houses. Allowing certain kinds of books, magazines and papers into the homes of christians will assuredly lead to sin, and if the houses of the saints are affected by leaven, we can be sure that it will slip into the assembly.

I do not think we should ever begin to count up our numbers at all. We can number the assemblies, but not the persons. Keep the number out of sight, because it is a day of small things, but a day of quality. And so the devil would spoil us, our little selves as I was saying, in these little meetings. These meetings are nothing at all in the eyes of the big men of this world, but they are everything in the eyes of heaven just now. I say everything because heaven is engaged with these meetings. They are the very centre of the divine operations. I do not hesitate to say that at all … we should make the most of them and … give priority to these meetings because they work out the purpose of God.

It is a very serious matter to despise the assembly of God and we do this if we allow any class distinction amongst us when we are assembled … In Corinth worldly principles were governing, which was something dreadful, and Paul must therefore say, “it is not to eat the Lord’s supper”, 1 Corinthians 11: 20. If we allow any person to rule in the assembly, we are giving place to Judas.
The anointing is for testimony, the sealing is for God, and the earnest is for us.

All promises look on to the world to come ... Promises refer to the earth; they involve the question of what God can do in an evil world. The purpose of God is beyond the promises. The promises serve to bring out what God can do, He is bringing in a world according to His own nature, and putting out a lawless world. It is an immense thing to have a sense in one’s own soul that God is able to perform that which He has promised. The power is resurrection—Christ risen from among the dead.
